questions.prompt: The interviewer says "Design a URL shortener." What should you do first?

options.text: Draw a load balancer, app servers and a database
Ask about features, scale and quality targets, and agree what's in scope

questions.explanation: Requirements turn a vague prompt into a concrete problem. Every later decision refers back to them.

questions.prompt: Which of these are non-functional requirements?

options.text: Users can choose a custom alias
The service is available 99.99% of the time
A created link is never lost

questions.explanation: Latency, availability and durability describe how well the system works. Custom aliases are a feature, so a functional requirement.

questions.prompt: You estimate 18,000 reads per second at peak. What makes this estimate useful?

options.text: Computing it to the exact request
Saying what it implies, for example that the database needs a cache in front of it
Converting it to requests per hour

questions.explanation: An estimate earns its place by driving a decision. Precision beyond the order of magnitude rarely matters.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest way to handle a deep dive into short-code generation?

options.text: Name a library that generates IDs
Compare random codes with a collision check and counter-based codes, then choose one with reasons tied to the requirements
Say it's a detail that doesn't matter

questions.explanation: Deep dives are where you show judgement: at least two options, their trade-offs, and a choice justified by your requirements.

questions.prompt: Near the end, you point out that your single cache cluster is a bottleneck at 10× traffic and explain how you'd shard it. How does this land?

options.text: Badly: it admits the design has a flaw
Well: finding and fixing your own design's limits is a senior signal
Neutral: interviewers only grade the diagram

questions.explanation: Every design has limits. Naming bottlenecks and failure modes yourself, with a plan, shows the judgement interviewers look for most.
